correctness.rationale: A noninterval has a component missing all maximum vertices of the cosine projection (the maximum vertices are a singleton or an adjacent pair). At a largest-weight vertex of that component, a step toward a nearest maximum strictly raises the weight and exits the component, hence exits the mask. For nonzero Z fix its argument and repeat these strict adjacent swaps. Finiteness forces an interval; the last noninterval is obtained by moving an interval endpoint one step outward, hence is a one-gap arc. If the starting mask is not one-gap, the first portion of this path strictly raises its projection above |Z(S)| and the final one-gap modulus bounds the raised value. A geometric sum plus the swapped endpoint gives R²=M²−4(sin²(kπ/N)−sin²(π/N)); the subtracted difference is positive by the sine product identity. For N≥6, R²=(1−4sin²(π/N))M²+4sin²(π/N)>0; for N=5 the size-two case and its complement have nonzero sums. For N=4 the only nonintervals are the two opposite pairs. In the interior range the unique longer occupied and vacancy runs distinguish the two orientations and forbid rotational stabilizers; for k=2 the distance-two pairs give N masks unless N=4, and complementation handles k=N−2. The unitary-basis Gram matrix has diagonals k/N and off-diagonal modulus |Z|/N, yielding the claimed sharp gap by rationalization. The frozen floating enumeration was inspected, not used as proof or rerun.

value.rationale: Once intervals are known optimal, the first attainable finite defect is a natural exact measure of rigidity for these erasure masks. Its equality geometry identifies the single-endpoint defect, with a full count including the degenerate cases. That is useful information not supplied by strictness of the unrestricted optimum or a continuous deficit bound.
residual_risks: No stability classification for other Fourier bands or arbitrary weights is implied.
